title: Kando Framework
subtitle: The systematic conversion of operational experience into strategic intelligence — and of raw operational data into genuine, verifiable customer value.

in_short.what: A way of turning what goes wrong (lost deals, complaints, churn, audit findings) into the next piece of work.
in_short.when: Throughout an engagement, and most of all when a company is under pressure and has to choose what to fix first.
in_short.get: One named constraint at a time, and the order in which to deal with it.

sections.heading: What Kando Means
sections.body:
Kando means creating value that genuinely exceeds expectations — not as a marketing claim, but as a measurable operational outcome. In the Attolloo context, it means delivering to the companies Attolloo works with what they could not access elsewhere: executive depth, regulatory intelligence, and a structured methodology that remains with the company after the engagement ends.

Kando is the answer to the question that closes every Polaris sprint: are we creating value that genuinely exceeds market expectations? It is not a sentiment measure. It is an operational outcome — verified by data, not asserted in marketing.

sections.heading: Learning From What Goes Wrong
sections.body:
Kando reframes how ventures relate to failure signals. Lost deals, complaints, churn and audit findings are not administrative costs. They are direct, unambiguous evidence of the gap between customer expectation and product reality.

Treated as intelligence events rather than administrative costs, these signals power a continuous product improvement engine. The company that listens to its failure data builds better products faster. The one that processes them as admin absorbs the cost — and repeats the mistake.

+++ The same logic in institutional sales

A lost deal is the most valuable negative event an early-stage company has. Which question in the security questionnaire could not be answered? At which stage of procurement did the buyer stop replying? For a company that competes with the established players, the same goes for a partner that said no, or a question from the regulator that took weeks to answer. Each answer becomes work for the next sprint.

sections.heading: What to Do First When a Company Is Under Pressure
sections.body:
When a venture is under operational or financial pressure, the Kando crisis protocol applies a specific, non-negotiable sequence — because the order of interventions matters as much as the interventions themselves:

+++ The five steps, and why the order matters

① IDENTIFY THE PRIMARY CONSTRAINT — The bottleneck with the lowest maximum throughput in the system.

② EXPLOIT THE CONSTRAINT — Get the most out of the bottleneck as it is, before spending anything. Take away the work that does not need to pass through it.

③ SUBORDINATE EVERYTHING ELSE — Every other process supports the constraint. Do not build capacity elsewhere first.

④ ELEVATE THE CONSTRAINT — Targeted investment, capacity extension, or outsourcing at the specific bottleneck, and only after the first three steps.

⑤ REPEAT — A new constraint takes its place. Find it and start again. Continuous improvement is the operational default, not a project.

The sequence is not arbitrary. Constraint logic dictates which intervention comes first.

sections.heading: Why Attolloo Works With Few Companies
sections.body:
Goldratt's Drum-Buffer-Rope was built for factories: pace the whole line to the bottleneck, protect the bottleneck with a buffer, and release new work only as fast as it can be absorbed. Kando applies the same logic to Attolloo itself, where the bottleneck is not a machine. It is the senior executive's attention.

DRUM — The executive's capacity for judgement: due diligence, strategic decisions, and stakeholder relationships. It sets the pace for everything else.

BUFFER — The 6Sense Filter. Only qualified ventures reach the executive, so that capacity is not spent on deals that should have been stopped earlier.

ROPE — Polaris Sprints. New engagements are taken in only as fast as the drum can carry them. The number of active engagements is set by that capacity, not by deal flow.

For a founder, the consequence is practical: the number of companies Attolloo works with at one time is limited by design.

sections.heading: When the Constraint Is a Person
sections.body:
In an early-stage company the constraint is usually one or two people: the founder, or the one specialist who can answer the regulator. The Kando steps apply to them as to any other bottleneck. First take away the work that does not need to pass through them. Only then add capacity.

A person is not a machine, though. Someone who never gets to step back makes worse decisions long before anything else shows, and a founder close to the wall is a governance risk. It belongs in the same register as a missing classification or an unmapped supplier, and it is handled the same way: named, given an owner, and followed up.

sections.heading: When Proof Becomes a Selling Point
sections.body:
In regulated sectors, verified transparency shifts willingness-to-pay. When a company can demonstrate — not just claim — regulatory compliance, data governance maturity, and AI integrity, that verification becomes a market positioning mechanism, not a compliance checkbox.

This is Kando in market-facing form: the value the customer perceives must be designed into the product and distribution model — not asserted in marketing copy. Audit trails and governance documentation are transparency assets that command premium pricing when genuine.
